71_marg1100: Without crime. If he had said “without sin,” no one could rightly be ordained a minister in the Church. For many baptized faithful are without crime; but without sin in this life I would say no one, not because any sin remains that is not remitted in baptism, but because in us, who remain in the weakness of this life, there do not cease to arise daily those things which are daily forgiven to those who pray faithfully. Examine however just a man as much as you like in this life, he is nevertheless not without sin. Whence John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” But plainly, many just men are called without complaint, which is understood as without crime. For no complaint is just against those who have no crime. Crime therefore is a complaint, that is, a grave sin most worthy of accusation and condemnation, such as murder, adultery, some uncleanness of fornication, theft, fraud, and the like; when a man begins not to have these, he begins to lift up his head toward liberty. But this liberty is begun, not perfect.

71_marg1101: The husband of one wife. After baptism, because to the new man neither fornications nor any things that were before are a hindrance. Augustine contradicts this opinion in these words: They understand more keenly who judged that neither the man who as a catechumen or pagan had another wife should be ordained, because it is a matter of the sacrament, not of sin. For in baptism all sins are forgiven. And he who said: “If a virgin marry, she hath not sinned,” sufficiently declared that marriage is not a sin. But for the sanctity of the sacrament, as a woman, if she was defiled as a catechumen, cannot after baptism be consecrated among the virgins of God, so it was seen, not absurdly, that the twice-married man has not sinned but has lost the rule of the sacrament, necessary not for the merit of life but for the seal of ecclesiastical ordination. And as many wives of the ancient fathers signified the churches that were to be from all nations, subject to one husband, that is, Christ, so our prelate, that is, the bishop, as the husband of one wife signifies the unity from all nations subject to one husband, Christ. And so, as it is not lawful “to serve two masters,” so it is not lawful to apostatize from the one God and go over to the superstition of another.

71_marg1106: One of them, etc. It is lawful to take from any source whatever testimony that one has found true, for the divine authority; as also Paul, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, when speaking to the Athenians, said of God: “In him we live, and move, and are; as some also of your own poets said.” And of the Athenian altar’s inscription he says: “I found an altar on which was written: To the unknown God.” So divine authority takes from wherever it finds what is necessary, but does not confirm that everything written there is to be accepted.
